title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI system generated a fake news article impersonating a real financial regulator and a real media personality, fabricating a detailed interview that never happened to promote an unlicensed investment platform. The system created a false assertion of endorsement from a public figure, which is a foundational technique in investment fraud. The deployment was used outside any legitimate purpose, as a tool in a criminal scam with no oversight or human authorization involved.

This failure happens at the point where AI-generated content reaches potential victims without verification. Catching it would have required either technical controls preventing impersonation of real people, platform policies blocking deepfakes before distribution, or human review of the content before it circulated. The scam works because fabricated articles and video deepfakes can be created at scale faster than they can be fact-checked or removed.

It is not established whether the AI systems used were general-purpose language models fine-tuned for this purpose, specialized deepfake tools, or both, nor is it established whether their developers knew they would be used this way.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fake online article claimed Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock had a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The interview never occurred. This fabricated story exemplifies a growing scam trend involving AI-generated deepfakes of celebrities and politicians used to promote fraudulent investments. ASIC research reveals these schemes are becoming more sophisticated and widespread, with the regulator removing 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase from the previous year.

Prominent Australians frequently impersonated include Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Alan Kohler, and billionaire Gina Rinehart. Scammers create elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, websites, and advertisements featuring fabricated endorsements. Potential victims see ads linking to fake articles, and once they provide details, scammers make follow-up calls and encourage investment in fake platforms. ASIC urges consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing, while presenter Kohler calls for heavy fines against platforms and AI models enabling these scams.
